key_facts: The chapter covers: Connectivity (Paths and Circuits), Euler and Hamilton Paths, the Shortest Path Problem (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Ford's algorithm), and Graph Coloring.
A cut vertex (articulation point) is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph; in Vietnamese: 'đỉnh cắt' hay 'điểm khớp'.
An Euler path is a path that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once; a Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once.
Shortest path algorithms covered include Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall algorithm.

The material is authored by Huynh Tuong Nguyen, Tran Tuan Anh, Nguyen An Khuong, and Le Hong Trang from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Technology - VNUHCM, dated August 16, 2021.
A Hamilton circuit is defined as a circuit that visits each vertex in a graph exactly once.

Three rules of Hamilton Circuits are taught: (Rule 1) if deg(v) = 2, both edges incident to v must be used; (Rule 2) no subcircuit can be formed; (Rule 3) once two edges at a vertex v are determined, all other edges incident at v must be removed.
Property of Dijkstra's Algorithm: applicable for any graph G with any edge length ℓ(vi) ≥ 0, one-to-all shortest paths, time complexity O(|V|²).
Dijkstra's algorithm CAN be used on directed graphs (digraphs), but CANNOT be used on graphs with negative edge weights.

An application of Hamilton circuits is generating Gray Code: an n-digit Gray code can be generated by finding Hamilton circuits of an n-dimensional hypercube; Gray code is used in digital communication to reduce the effect of noise.
generated_text: Introduction to Graph Connectivity Welcome to the study of Graph Connectivity. In many real-world problems, from designing reliable computer networks to planning efficient delivery routes, we need to understand how different points in a system are connected. This lesson explores the fundamental concepts of paths, circuits, and the overall connectedness of graphs. We will define what it means for a graph to be connected, learn how to measure its resilience, and investigate two famous problems: traversing every edge (Euler paths) and visiting every vertex (Hamilton paths). 1. Paths, Circuits, and Basic Connectivity The most basic way to understand connectivity is by looking at how we can travel from one vertex to another. Paths and Circuits In graph theory, we formalize the idea of a route with the concepts of paths and circuits. Path: A path of length n from a vertex u to a vertex v in an undirected graph is a sequence of n edges connecting a sequence of vertices. For example, a path from x₀ to xₙ is represented by the edges {x₀, x₁}, {x₁, x₂}, ..., {xₙ₋₁, xₙ}. The length is the number of edges in the path. Circuit: A circuit is a path that begins and ends at the same vertex (i.e., u = v). Simple Path/Circuit: A path or circuit is called simple if it does not contain the same edge more than once. In directed graphs, a path is similarly a sequence of edges, but the direction of the edges must be followed, for instance: (x₀, x₁), (x₁, x₂), ..., (xₙ₋₁, xₙ). Connectedness in Undirected Graphs Now we can use the concept of a path to define what it means for a whole graph to be connected. An undirected graph is called connected if there is a path between every pair of distinct vertices in the graph. A key property is that if a graph is connected, there is also a simple path between every pair of distinct vertices. If a graph is not connected, it is called disconnected . A disconnected graph is composed of two or more connected components , which are the maximal connected subgraphs. 2. How Connected is a Graph? Some graphs are more robustly connected than others. Removing a single vertex or edge might break a graph into multiple components. We have special terms for these critical points. Identifying Critical Points and Edges Cut Vertex (or Articulation Point): A vertex whose removal (along with its incident edges) increases the number of connected components in a graph. Cut Edge (or Bridge): An edge whose removal increases the number of connected components in a graph. Quantifying Connectivity We can measure the connectivity of a graph by determining the minimum number of vertices or edges that need to be removed to disconnect it. A vertex cut is a set of vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. The vertex connectivity , denoted κ(G), is the minimum number of vertices in a vertex cut. An edge cut is a set of edges whose removal disconnects the graph. The edge connectivity , denoted λ(G), is the minimum number of edges in an edge cut. A graph that has no cut vertices is called a nonseparable graph . Real-World Applications Vertex and edge connectivity are crucial for assessing the reliability of networks. For example, in a communication network, vertex connectivity can represent the minimum number of routers that must fail to disconnect the network. Edge connectivity can represent the minimum number of links that must go down to cause a disconnection. 3. Connectivity in Directed Graphs For directed graphs, we must consider the direction of edges, leading to two levels of connectivity. A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a path from any vertex a to any other vertex b , AND a path from b back to a . A directed graph is weakly connected if there is a path between any two vertices in the underlying undirected graph (i.e., ignoring the direction of the edges). 4. Special Types of Paths and Circuits Two historical problems in graph theory led to the study of special kinds of paths and circuits that traverse a graph in a specific way. Euler Paths and Circuits This concept originated from the famous Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem, which asked if one could walk through the city, crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. An Euler path is a simple path in a graph that traverses every edge exactly once. An Euler circuit is an Euler path that is also a circuit, meaning it starts and ends at the same vertex. A connected multigraph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has an even degree. It has an Euler path if and only if it has exactly two vertices of odd degree, or no vertices of odd degree. Hamilton Paths and Circuits This concept is related to the Traveling Salesman Problem , which seeks the shortest possible route that visits a set of cities and returns to the origin city. A Hamilton circuit is a simple circuit in a graph that passes through every vertex exactly once. A Hamilton path is a simple path that passes through every vertex exactly once. Unlike Euler circuits, there is no simple necessary and sufficient condition to determine if a graph has a Hamilton circuit. However, some rules can help in finding one, such as noting that if a vertex has a degree of 2, both of its incident edges must be part of any Hamilton circuit. Summary This lesson covered the core concepts of graph connectivity. Here are the key takeaways: A path is a sequence of edges, and a circuit is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex. A graph is connected if there is a path between any two of its vertices. Cut vertices and cut edges are critical points whose removal can disconnect a graph. Vertex connectivity (κ(G)) and edge connectivity (λ(G)) measure how robustly a graph is connected. Directed graphs can be strongly connected (paths exist in both directions) or weakly connected (connected if directions are ignored). An Euler path/circuit traverses every edge exactly once. Its existence depends on the degree of the vertices. A Hamilton path/circuit visits every vertex exactly once. There is no simple formula for determining its existence.
